Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Vignette:
At thirty-five, Thien Nguyen worked as a UX designer in a glass-walled studio where user testing sessions hummed with rhythmic mouse clicks and overlapping voices. His life shifted during a critical illness when he was twenty-nine. It began as a tightening pressure in his chest that escalated into breath-stealing pain while he sat at his drafting table. While his team moved through the open floor, Thien remained fixed, watching the clock as diagnostic results arrived in slow succession. The prolonged waits in the emergency department felt particularly potent; every pause in the medical team’s movements signaled to him that his condition was worsening. When the intravenous line was finally secured and the treatment took hold, the acute crisis receded, but the experience had permanently altered how he navigated his days. Over the following months, Thien’s routine narrowed to a careful accounting of physical cues and environmental rhythms. He developed a clear pattern of avoiding medical environments, deliberately routing his commute past urgent care centers and steering clear of hospital parking lots and parked ambulances. When physical examinations were scheduled, the press of a cold stethoscope against his torso or the steady compression of a sphygmomanometer cuff triggered an immediate readiness in his muscles. He avoided situations that put his body under stress, declining weekend jogs and long conference calls that required sustained posture, and he kept his thoughts tightly contained, sidestepping the illness episode entirely. His body remained constantly tense, coiled and prepared to react to any sudden shift. Even as his clinical markers normalized, he found it impossible to believe the reassurances offered by his colleagues and his wife, Clara. When Clara told him his recovery was complete, he accepted her words but felt a persistent distance between her certainty and his own internal state. He had come to believe there was something wrong with him as a person, a quiet defect that might surface without warning. He moved through his shared apartment and his professional duties with a steady emotional numbness, feeling dead inside, as though his responses had been muted. To him, he was simply a weak person, fragile alongside his other adjustments. The studio’s open layout, once a source of creative momentum, now felt like an exposure chamber. Every delayed software update or postponed meeting confirmation tightened his stomach. When a design review ran ten minutes past the scheduled hour, his shoulders tightened and his breath shallowed; he assumed something bad was happening, echoing the delayed diagnoses that had once trapped him in a hospital bed. In the usability labs where he spent his days mapping customer journeys, he began to withdraw from live testing sessions, preferring to observe from his desk rather than sit in the glass booths where monitors flickered and voices overlapped. He missed a key product launch because he could not bear the physical stress of airport travel, choosing instead to delegate his responsibilities while he remained at home. Clara noticed the quiet distance between them, how he would sit motionless while she spoke, his attention fixed inward, how he flinched at the sound of the refrigerator cycling or the sudden delivery of a diagnostic email. He would often pause before checking his own pulse, searching for a rhythm that felt reliable. The quiet accumulation of these daily adjustments had left him with a sense of waiting, as though he were still suspended in the moments before the diagnosis. What finally brought Thien to seek help was not a new medical crisis, but the exhaustion of living in a perpetual state of readiness. His intake assessment registered a PCL-5 score of 73, corresponding to the breadth of his symptoms. He recognized that he avoided medical cues, that he kept his thoughts guarded, and that his body felt constantly alert. He came to the clinic hoping to understand why his own weakness felt so unyielding, and what he might do to stop bracing for a threat that has already passed.
